deck.name: LLM Vocabulary
deck.description: Key terms for working with large language models.

questions.prompt: In a text-based LLM, what is a token?
choices: A text unit represented by a model token ID
A sentence encoded as a single embedding
A learned coefficient stored in the model
A hidden instruction supplied with a request
questions.explanation: Text tokens can be words, word pieces, punctuation or other text units.

choices: The number of model weights loaded into GPU memory
The elapsed time allowed for a response to finish
The token capacity available for one model input and response
The total number of documents in the training corpus
questions.explanation: Context limits and how input and output share them depend on the model.

choices: Plausible output that is incorrect or unsupported
A refusal to provide an answer to a request
A response that takes longer than expected to arrive
An answer cut short by the output token limit
questions.explanation: Fluent wording does not establish factual accuracy.

questions.prompt: What does raising the "temperature" setting usually do?
choices: Makes the context window larger
Makes stored model weights smaller
Makes the training dataset broader
Makes token sampling more varied
questions.explanation: Temperature changes the token probability distribution used for sampling; it does not guarantee correctness.

choices: Sampling from a probability-mass cutoff set of tokens
Sampling from a fixed number of top-ranked tokens
Always selecting the single highest-probability token
Rejecting replies longer than a fixed token count
questions.explanation: Top-p uses a cumulative probability threshold. Top-k instead limits the candidate count.

choices: A numerical vector representing features of an input
A text sequence containing instructions for a task
A probability score for a complete generated response
A compressed copy of a trained model weight file
questions.explanation: Embedding similarity can help retrieval, but similarity is not proof that a source answers a question.

questions.prompt: Which 2017 paper introduced the Transformer architecture?
choices: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Attention Is All You Need
Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
Generative Adversarial Nets
questions.explanation: The 2017 paper introduced the Transformer architecture using attention without recurrent layers.

questions.prompt: What does the attention mechanism let a model do?
choices: Keep permanent memories without external storage
Weight information from different token positions
Look up current information without retrieval tools
Update trained weights during every ordinary reply
questions.explanation: Attention combines representations using learned relevance scores. It does not itself provide web access.

choices: Initial training on broad data to learn general patterns
Evaluation on held-out data to compare final models
Request-time examples used to describe the task
Compression of trained weights to reduce precision
questions.explanation: Autoregressive text models commonly learn by predicting the next token. Other pretraining objectives also exist.

choices: Changing sampling settings for one model request
Retrieving documents to place beside a user prompt
Reducing numerical precision to store model weights
Further training of an already pretrained model
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning changes learned weights. Prompting and retrieval usually leave them unchanged.
Human preference ratings train a reward model, which then guides further training.

choices: The first ordinary user question in a conversation
An example answer supplied for a demonstration task
The saved conversation returned by a retrieval search
High-priority instructions supplied to shape model behavior
questions.explanation: A system prompt is an instruction mechanism, not a guarantee that every request will be followed correctly.

choices: Training a model with a small number of new weights
Combining a small set of separately trained models
Sampling a small number of possible response tokens
Including a small set of task examples in the prompt
questions.explanation: Zero-shot prompting supplies no task demonstrations. Few-shot examples guide behavior without retraining.

choices: Repeating the same request in several languages
Prompting for intermediate reasoning steps
Retrieving related documents before generating text
Training successive models on the same dataset
questions.explanation: The technique was studied in Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models.

choices: Retrieving information to inform a generated answer
Training a model to permanently memorize new pages
Quantizing model weights before serving a response
Averaging outputs from independently trained models
questions.explanation: Retrieval supplies external context. The model can still misread it or make unsupported claims.

questions.prompt: What is a vector database typically used for in LLM apps?
choices: Storing model weights and executing neural layers
Storing vectors and searching for similar vectors
Storing API credentials and authenticating requests
Storing token IDs and splitting text into word pieces
questions.explanation: Vector similarity supports semantic retrieval; many apps combine it with keyword search or filters.

choices: Request settings that control token sampling
Text examples supplied in the current prompt
Documents retrieved for the current question
Learned numerical values within the network
questions.explanation: Weights are learned during training, while settings such as temperature are chosen for inference.

choices: Updating a model from a training dataset
Assigning target labels to training examples
Using a trained model to produce an output
Scoring a model against a held-out benchmark
questions.explanation: Ordinary inference uses trained weights without running a training update.

choices: Converts a model into lower-precision weights
Converts relevant documents into search rankings
Converts text into token IDs and back
Converts user requests into authenticated API calls
questions.explanation: The tokenizer defines text segmentation and its token vocabulary. Different models may count the same text differently.

choices: Reducing the number of examples in a training batch
Representing model values at lower numerical precision
Removing repeated documents from a training corpus
Limiting the maximum length of a generated answer
questions.explanation: Quantization can reduce memory use. Effects on accuracy and speed depend on the method and hardware.

choices: Combining several models by averaging their weights
Compressing model weights into lower-bit formats
Retrieving text from a smaller document collection
Training a student model using a teacher model
questions.explanation: The student learns from teacher outputs or representations; it is often smaller or cheaper to run.

choices: Retrieving a few documents before each model request
Training low-rank updates while freezing base weights
Lowering the precision used to store all model weights
Training every weight again on a small task dataset
questions.explanation: LoRA is parameter-efficient fine-tuning. It learns small update matrices rather than replacing every base weight.

questions.prompt: In LLM apps, what is "tool use" (function calling)?
choices: Executing every proposed function without application code
Producing a structured request for an external function
Changing model weights by editing a function signature
Retrieving training examples from the model weights
questions.explanation: The application validates and executes tool calls, then can return results to the model.

questions.prompt: What is an "agent" in the LLM sense?
choices: A fixed template that formats one completed response
A database that stores vectors for similarity search
A tokenizer that converts user text into model IDs
A model-driven system that chooses and takes actions
questions.explanation: Agent designs vary. A common pattern uses tools and repeated steps to work toward a task.

questions.prompt: What is a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture?
choices: Averaging complete replies from several separate chatbots
Dividing a prompt into equal independent text chunks
Training one network only on expert-written examples
Routing inputs to a subset of specialized networks
questions.explanation: Sparse mixture-of-experts activates selected experts, so total parameter count differs from parameters used per token.

questions.prompt: What does "perplexity" measure for a language model?
choices: How clearly human reviewers understand its responses
How surprising evaluation text is under the model
How quickly the model produces each output token
How much GPU memory is needed to store its weights
questions.explanation: Lower perplexity means better prediction on comparable data. Comparisons require compatible tokenization and evaluation.

questions.prompt: Setting temperature to 0 makes the model pick the most likely token at each step, so outputs become close to deterministic.
questions.explanation: Small differences can still occur because of how the computation is run.

choices: Reducing temperature to make every answer factual
Basing an answer on identifiable supporting information
Keeping a model running entirely on local hardware
Training a model only on geographical information
questions.explanation: Grounding makes claims easier to check; it does not remove the need to verify that the sources support them.

questions.prompt: What is "latency" in an LLM service?
questions.answer: The time between sending a request and getting a response, often measured to the first token.

questions.prompt: A larger context window means the model has more parameters.
questions.explanation: Context length and parameter count are separate design choices.
